about.author: Zyphullen

automatic_checks.what: Structural checks run by a script on every build (src/audit.py, report in AUDIT-v0.8.md): every card has a colour and at least one source, links point at cards that exist, share links are exact, the data hash is the same in every file, counts match, and every source URL was fetched to see that it answers.
automatic_checks.not: They do not read the science. Passing them does not mean a claim is right, only that it is labelled, sourced and linked.

science_review.what: A science review means a person with the right expertise reads each claim against its sources and decides whether it is right, up to date and fairly coloured.
science_review.how_to_help: Every card has a Suggest a fix button (e-mail). Please check claims against the listed sources and say what looks wrong.

about.certainty_rule: green = established (known science, or a defined / proved result in Maths); orange = leading idea / partial progress; red = unknown / open problem. A link takes the colour of its less-certain end.

suggest_a_fix.subject: Echo Atlas fix: <Card name> (<card id>)
suggest_a_fix.note: Every card has a Suggest a fix button that opens a prefilled e-mail (section, card, card id, version, page link). Card ids: fntu/<id>, maths/<id>, history/<id>-<n>, cell/<id>, body/<id>, element/<symbol>, <section>/link/<from>><to>.

about.what_this_file_holds: A typical human cell: organelles, molecules, atoms and living processes, drawn to scale where possible.
about.already_in_this_file: This file already holds everything for this section: the facts (summary, details), the colours (certainty), the sources (title, url, type, year, link check) and the connections between ideas, including links to cards in other sections (rel / related / section_links, each with the other section name and id). Load another section file only when you want the full card on the other end of a link.
about.how_to_use: Every item has id, title, certainty, summary, details and sources (title, url, type). Full source details (year, link check) are in sources_used. A link's reason_sources are the sources on its two cards. Fact-check against the sources; flag anything that looks wrong or out of date.

virtual_cell.title: Typical human cell (generalised)
summary: A general human body cell, about 20 µm across: it has the parts most human cells share.
No single real cell type looks exactly like this; the shape is simplified.
details: Real human cells range from about 7 µm (red blood cells) to over 100 µm, and from round to long and branched.
Sizes and speeds of the parts inside are real measured values, drawn to scale.
Some counts are reduced so you can see between things: proteins at ~1/8 of real crowding, 30 of ~10,000 vaults, fewer microtubules and ribosomes.

virtual_cell.title: Cell membrane
summary: A skin of fat molecules two layers thick, about 5 nm.
It lets some things in and keeps others out.
details: Made of roughly a billion lipid molecules, with proteins floating in it.
In cells that crawl, the front edge ruffles and moves forward a few µm per minute (a lamellipodium).
Zoom right in to see the two layers of lipids.

sources.title: Singer & Nicolson 1972: The Fluid Mosaic Model of the Structure of Cell Membranes (Science)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 3.1 The Cell Membrane

virtual_cell.title: Nucleus
summary: The control centre: about 10 × 8 µm here (typically 5–10 µm).
It holds 46 chromosomes: about 2 metres of DNA.
details: About 6.2 billion DNA letters (base pairs) in two copies of the genome.
Wrapped in a double membrane with a few thousand pores.
Under a microscope (🔬 button) it glows blue, like the DAPI dye biologists use to stain DNA.

sources.title: International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium 2001: Initial sequencing and analysis of the human genome (Nature)
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 3.3 The Nucleus and DNA Replication

virtual_cell.title: Chromatin (DNA)
summary: DNA wound on protein spools (nucleosomes).
Each spool holds 147 DNA letters, wrapped almost twice.
details: A nucleosome is about 11 nm wide and made of 8 histone proteins.
About 30 million nucleosomes pack the genome into the nucleus.
In living cells the beads fold into irregular chains 5–24 nm wide, not a neat uniform 30 nm fibre.

sources.title: Ou et al. 2017: ChromEMT: Visualizing 3D chromatin structure and compaction in interphase and mitotic cells (Science)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 14.2 DNA Structure and Sequencing

virtual_cell.title: Nucleosome
summary: A spool of 8 histone proteins with DNA wrapped around it.
About 11 nm wide.
details: 147 base pairs wrap about 1.65 turns.
Linker DNA joins one spool to the next, like beads on a string.
Drawn simplified: DNA wrapped around histone beads. The two twisted strands are the 2 nm double helix; the wrapping around each bead is not drawn.

sources.title: Luger et al. 1997: Crystal structure of the nucleosome core particle at 2.8 Å resolution (Nature)
Ou et al. 2017: ChromEMT: Visualizing 3D chromatin structure and compaction in interphase and mitotic cells (Science)

virtual_cell.title: Nucleolus
summary: A dense spot inside the nucleus, 1–3 µm.
It builds the parts of ribosomes.
details: Most human cells have 1–4. It has no membrane: it forms where ribosome genes cluster.
Ribosome pieces leave through the nuclear pores.

sources.title: Boisvert et al. 2007: The multifunctional nucleolus (Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol)

virtual_cell.title: Nuclear pore
summary: A gate in the nucleus wall, about 120 nm across.
mRNA goes out, proteins come in.
details: One of the biggest machines in the cell: ~1,000 proteins of ~30 kinds, in 8-fold symmetry.
A human nucleus has roughly 2,000–5,000 pores.

sources.title: Kim et al. 2018: Integrative structure and functional anatomy of a nuclear pore complex (Nature)

virtual_cell.title: Ribosome
summary: A protein-building machine, about 25–30 nm.
It reads mRNA and adds about 5–6 amino acids per second.
details: A human cell has millions (estimates around 10 million in fast-growing cells).
Two parts: a small (40S) and a large (60S) subunit.
At 1× speed you can watch the new chain grow at the real rate.

virtual_cell.title: Endoplasmic reticulum
summary: A lace of tubes and sheets spreading through the cell.
Makes proteins and fats, stores calcium.
details: Rough ER (with ribosomes) sits near the nucleus; smooth tubes reach out to the edge.
Tubes are about 50–100 nm wide and keep moving and re-joining.

sources.title: Palade 1975: Intracellular Aspects of the Process of Protein Synthesis (Science)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.4 The Endomembrane System and Proteins

virtual_cell.title: Golgi apparatus
summary: Stacks of flat sacs next to the nucleus: the post office.
It sorts, tags and packs proteins.
details: In human cells the stacks join into a ribbon of several µm near the centrosome.
Each stack has about 4–8 sacs (cisternae).
Cells that secrete a lot, like fibroblasts making collagen, have big Golgi.

sources.title: Palade 1975: Intracellular Aspects of the Process of Protein Synthesis (Science)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.4 The Endomembrane System and Proteins

virtual_cell.title: Vesicle
summary: A small bubble (50–100 nm) carrying cargo.
Motor proteins walk it along microtubules at about 1 µm per second.
details: Kinesin walks outwards (~0.8 µm/s), dynein inwards (~1 µm/s).
Off the track, a vesicle only jiggles slowly: the cytoplasm is very crowded.

sources.title: Novick et al. 1980: Identification of 23 complementation groups required for post-translational events in the yeast secretory pathway (Cell)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.4 The Endomembrane System and Proteins

virtual_cell.title: Mitochondrion
summary: The power station: makes ATP.
A tube about 0.5 µm wide and 1–10 µm long; a human cell has hundreds.
details: They form a network that splits and joins every few minutes.
The folds inside (cristae) hold ATP synthase, a spinning motor.
It has its own small DNA: it came from a bacterium long ago.

sources.title: Mitchell 1961: Coupling of Phosphorylation to Electron and Hydrogen Transfer by a Chemi-Osmotic type of Mechanism (Nature)

virtual_cell.title: ATP synthase
summary: A rotary motor about 10 nm wide in the cristae.
It spins over 100 times a second to make ATP.
details: Protons flowing through it turn the rotor.
Each turn makes 3 ATP.

sources.title: Abrahams et al. 1994: Structure at 2.8 Å resolution of F1-ATPase from bovine heart mitochondria (Nature)
Noji et al. 1997: Direct observation of the rotation of F1-ATPase (Nature)

virtual_cell.title: ATP
summary: The cell’s energy coin.
Made in mitochondria, spent everywhere.
details: A human body makes and recycles roughly its own weight in ATP every day.

virtual_cell.title: Lysosome
summary: A recycling bag full of enzymes, 0.1–1 µm.
A cell has a few hundred.
details: Its inside is acidic (pH about 4.5–5); a pump uses ATP to push protons in.
Its enzymes work best in acid, so any that leak into the near-neutral cytoplasm (pH ~7.2) do little harm.

sources.title: de Duve et al. 1955: Tissue fractionation studies. 6. Intracellular distribution patterns of enzymes in rat-liver tissue (Biochemical Journal)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.4 The Endomembrane System and Proteins

virtual_cell.title: Peroxisome
summary: A small bag (0.1–0.5 µm) that burns fats.
It makes and destroys hydrogen peroxide.
details: Human cells have a few hundred.
Also helps make some special fats for the brain.

sources.title: De Duve & Baudhuin 1966: Peroxisomes (microbodies and related particles). (Physiological Reviews)

virtual_cell.title: Lipid droplet
summary: A store of fat, 0.5–2 µm.
Wrapped in a single layer of lipids.
details: Cells use them as an energy store and to make membranes.

sources.title: Walther & Farese 2012: Lipid Droplets and Cellular Lipid Metabolism (Annu. Rev. Biochem.)

virtual_cell.title: Centrosome
summary: Two tiny barrels (centrioles), 250 nm wide and 500 nm long.
Microtubules grow out from here.
details: Each barrel is 9 groups of 3 tubes.
In most human cells the older barrel also grows a primary cilium, a tiny antenna.
It helps pull chromosomes apart when the cell divides.

virtual_cell.title: Microtubule
summary: Hollow tubes 25 nm wide: roads and scaffolding.
Each tip grows ~12 µm/min, then suddenly shrinks.
details: This "dynamic instability" is simulated here with measured rates.
The bright tip is where new tubulin is added (biologists see it with EB1 tags).
Kinesin and dynein walk on them carrying cargo.

sources.title: Nogales et al. 1998: Structure of the αβ tubulin dimer by electron crystallography (Nature)

virtual_cell.title: Actin stress fibres
summary: Bundles of actin filaments (each 7 nm) running across the cell.
They pull on the ground like ropes.
details: They end at focal adhesions, the cell’s "feet".
A single filament is two strands twisted, crossing every 37 nm.

sources.title: Kabsch et al. 1990: Atomic structure of the actin: DNase I complex (Nature)

virtual_cell.title: Focal adhesion
summary: A cell’s “foot” that grips the surface, 1–5 µm long.
Stress fibres pull on it.
details: Made of integrins and many linking proteins.
Feet at the front form and mature in minutes.

sources.title: Geiger et al. 2001: Transmembrane crosstalk between the extracellular matrix and the cytoskeleton (Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol)

virtual_cell.title: Vimentin filaments
summary: Rope-like filaments, 10 nm wide.
They cushion the nucleus and help the cell resist stretching.
details: Vimentin is the main intermediate filament of many cell types (e.g. fibroblasts); others use keratins.

sources.title: Herrmann et al. 2007: Intermediate filaments: from cell architecture to nanomechanics (Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol)

virtual_cell.title: Vault
summary: A hollow barrel of protein and RNA, about 40 × 70 nm.
What it does is still not clear.
details: About 10,000 per cell (some cells have more).
Ideas include transport or defence, but no job is proven.

sources.title: Kedersha & Rome 1986: Isolation and characterization of a novel ribonucleoprotein particle: large structures contain a single species of small RNA. (The Journal of cell biology)
Tanaka et al. 2009: The Structure of Rat Liver Vault at 3.5 Angstrom Resolution (Science)

virtual_cell.title: Cytosol
summary: The gel that fills the cell: about 70% water.
Packed with roughly 3 million proteins per cubic µm.
details: So crowded that big things barely drift unless motors carry them.
Small molecules still diffuse fast: across the cell in seconds.

virtual_cell.title: Water molecule
summary: One oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms (H₂O).
About 99 of every 100 molecules in a cell are water.
details: Real water molecules jiggle and tumble trillions of times a second; here they are shown frozen or hugely slowed.
Water’s slightly charged ends help proteins fold.

virtual_cell.title: Glucose
summary: A sugar: a ring of carbon and oxygen.
Cells break it down for energy.
details: Glycolysis in the cytosol starts the job; mitochondria finish it and make ATP.

virtual_cell.title: Phospholipid
summary: A water-loving head and two oily tails, about 2.5 nm long.
Two layers of them make every membrane.
details: The tails hide from water, so lipids form two layers by themselves.
A kink in one tail keeps the membrane fluid.

sources.title: Singer & Nicolson 1972: The Fluid Mosaic Model of the Structure of Cell Membranes (Science)

virtual_cell.title: Base pair (DNA)
summary: Two DNA letters joined in the middle.
Each side hangs on a sugar-phosphate backbone.
details: A pairs with T, G pairs with C, held by weak hydrogen bonds.
Pairs are stacked 0.34 nm apart along the helix.

sources.title: Watson & Crick 1953: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid (Nature)
OpenStax Biology 2e, 14.2 DNA Structure and Sequencing

virtual_cell.title: Protein chain
summary: Amino acids linked in a chain by a ribosome.
The chain then folds into a working shape.
details: There are 20 kinds of amino acid; the gene sets their order.
The backbone repeats N–C–C; side chains stick out.

sources.title: Pauling et al. 1951: The structure of proteins: Two hydrogen-bonded helical configurations of the polypeptide chain (Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.)

virtual_cell.title: Protein
summary: A folded chain of thousands of atoms, typically 3–10 nm.
Proteins do most of the work in a cell.
details: Enzymes, motors, pumps and scaffolds are all proteins.
Shown as simple blobs: real shapes are far more detailed.

sources.title: Milo 2013: What is the total number of protein molecules per cell volume? A call to rethink some published values (BioEssays)

virtual_cell.title: Hydrogen atom
summary: The smallest atom: 1 proton, 1 electron.
Made just after the Big Bang.
details: About 6 in 10 atoms in your body are hydrogen.

sources.title: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 2.3 Atomic Structure and Symbolism

virtual_cell.title: Carbon atom
summary: 6 protons. The backbone of life’s molecules.
Made inside stars.
details: Carbon can bond to four other atoms, so it builds chains and rings.

virtual_cell.title: Nitrogen atom
summary: 7 protons.
Found in every amino acid and DNA letter.
details: Made inside stars (the CNO cycle).

sources.title: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 2.3 Atomic Structure and Symbolism

virtual_cell.title: Oxygen atom
summary: 8 protons.
In water, sugars and the phosphate groups of ATP.
details: By mass, most of your body is oxygen (in water).

sources.title: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 2.3 Atomic Structure and Symbolism

virtual_cell.title: Phosphorus atom
summary: 15 protons.
At the heart of ATP, DNA’s backbone and membrane lipids.
details: Made in massive stars and spread by supernovae.

sources.title: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 2.3 Atomic Structure and Symbolism

virtual_cell.title: Electron cloud
summary: Electrons are not little planets.
The cloud shows where an electron is likely to be found.
details: This comes from quantum mechanics (orbitals).
An atom is almost all empty space.

sources.title: Schrödinger 1926: An Undulatory Theory of the Mechanics of Atoms and Molecules (Phys. Rev.)
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 6.3 Development of Quantum Theory

virtual_cell.title: Atomic nucleus
summary: Protons and neutrons packed tight.
It holds over 99.9% of the atom’s mass.
details: Really about 100,000 times smaller than the atom; drawn far too big here.
Protons and neutrons are made of quarks.

sources.title: Rutherford 1911: The scattering of α and β particles by matter and the structure of the atom (Philosophical Magazine)
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 21.1 Nuclear Structure and Stability
